newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS- Copper joins coffee in commodity advance.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS- Copper joins coffee in commodity advance.

text.p: Profit-taking braked prices for coffee futures on Friday after their relentless rally had seen one New York contract hit a 20-year high.
Elsewhere, copper chalked up an 11-1/2 month high on the London Metal Exchange but gold eased on German bullion reserve revaluation fears and a sell-off in silver.
A volatile mix of low stocks, tight Latin American supply and worries that Brazil may have another frost has sent coffee futures on their longest sustained rally for two decades.
Both Brazil and Colombia, the two biggest coffee producing nations, this week said they faced production deficits and would have to meet export commitments by digging into stocks.
Spot May futures for the mainly South American grown arabica beans traded at $2.79 cents per pound in New York on Thursday, the highest since June 1977.
Some analysts said the spot month was not truly representative, but the July contract - on which there is most interest - is also dramatically up, by almost 125 percent this year.
July hit $2.62 on Thursday but traded as low as $2.45 during Friday on commission house profit-taking.
London futures for robusta beans, grown in Asia and Africa and used mainly for soluble or instant blends, have followed New York to jump 65 percent since the start of the year.
The benchmark London July contract hit a 15-month high of $2,060 per tonne, breaking $2,000 for the first time this year despite robustas being in more generous supply.

French coffee drinkers were the latest to feel the pinch of new price rises in the shops as producers, set to meet for talks in London next week, feared price rises would make consumers turn to tea or soft drinks instead.
The German coffee industry association DKV said high futures prices and a strong dollar were inflating roasters' costs and made further retail price hikes look inevitable.
Indonesia, the number three seller, said that the producers led by Brazil should show that "we are not a cartel".
Concerns that high prices may depress demand for coffee will be aired in London next week at talks among 62 producing and consumer nations within the International Coffee Organization.

At parallel sessions, growers in their 14-nation Association of Coffee Producing Countries may defer plans to extend export quotas that were designed to keep a floor under world prices when these sagged last year.
Precious metals turned lower on Friday.
Gold, sentiment towards it shredded by news that the Germans may revalue their bullion reserves in a move linked to their budget deficit, sank with silver.
Gold slipped to a London fix at $344.50 an ounce, down $2.50 from the morning compared to $346.40 on Thursday.
Frail market confidence has been sternly tested since Wednesday night when rumours that Germany was considering revaluing its reserves first emerged.
"This is a structural change for the market," said Union Bank of Switzerland bullion market analyst Andy Smith.
Dealers said the long term risk for the market was that gold would now be treated like any other asset which would be sold if it didn't earn its keep.
Silver had bounced up to its highest fixing since April 2 this year at $4.8735 on Wednesday, but eased to $4.7173 per ounce on speculative selling during London's Friday afternoon.
Copper hit an 11-1/2 month high of $2,488 a tonne early on Friday only to settle during the day and close marginally ahead at $2,466.
"I'm very friendly towards copper, but things are going to get more difficult in the $2,480-$2,520 area," one trader said.
A 2,400-tonne drawdown in LME stocks also suggested further upside attempts, as did a possibility of a strike by Chilean copper workers against a proposal to privatise state companies.
Wheat futures on the Chicago Board of Trade were up a couple of cents a bushel, partly on a dry weather outlook.
